# Visualization mapping
## Overview
Visualization mapping translates volumetric data values and derived features into optical properties and visual styles to resolve visual ambiguity in 3D datasets [G]. It determines which structures are visible, how they appear, and how users interact with the representation [G]. This family focuses specifically on the mathematical and algorithmic mapping from data space to visual space, distinct from data representation [2-volume-data-and-representation.md](2-volume-data-and-representation.md) and rendering algorithms [16-image-order-rendering.md](16-image-order-rendering.md), [22-object-order-rendering.md](22-object-order-rendering.md) [G]. It operates on continuous volumetric samples rather than discrete isosurfaces [29-surface-extraction.md](29-surface-extraction.md), and prioritizes perceptual clarity and feature emphasis over strict physical accuracy [32-light-transport-in-participating-media.md](32-light-transport-in-participating-media.md) [G].
## Shared principles
All methods evaluate a mapping function at sample points $\mathbf{x}$ within the volume to produce visual attributes [G]. The core mechanism involves:
1. **Input Evaluation**: Sampling the data field $f(\mathbf{x})$ and potentially derived features (e.g., gradients, eigenvalues) at position $\mathbf{x}$ [G].
2. **Mapping**: Applying a function to convert these inputs into visual parameters [G]. For scalar data, this yields opacity $\alpha \in [0, 1]$ and color $\mathbf{c} \in [0, 1]^3$ [38-classification-and-transfer-functions.md](38-classification-and-transfer-functions.md). For vector/tensor data, it yields directional cues or geometric primitives [39-multi-field-vector-and-tensor-volume-visualization.md](39-multi-field-vector-and-tensor-volume-visualization.md).
3. **Integration**: These parameters modulate the contribution of each sample during the rendering pass [G].
4. **Feedback**: In interactive contexts, user inputs modify the mapping parameters in real-time [41-interaction.md](41-interaction.md).
## Subtopics

### [Classification and transfer functions](38-classification-and-transfer-functions.md)
Maps scalar data values and derived features to optical properties, primarily color and opacity, to determine visibility and appearance [38-classification-and-transfer-functions.md](38-classification-and-transfer-functions.md). It sets itself apart by focusing on the mathematical and algorithmic mapping from data space to visual space, using structures like piecewise linear functions and lookup tables. Choose this for standard direct volume rendering of scalar datasets.

### [Multi-field, vector and tensor volume visualization](39-multi-field-vector-and-tensor-volume-visualization.md)
Maps non-scalar data attributes (direction, magnitude, phase) to visual properties, solving the problem of representing directional, anisotropic, or phase-dependent information [39-multi-field-vector-and-tensor-volume-visualization.md](39-multi-field-vector-and-tensor-volume-visualization.md). It differs by encoding field structure through geometric or color-based mappings rather than artistic style. Choose this for vector, tensor, or complex-valued volumetric data.

### [Illustrative and non-photorealistic volume rendering](40-illustrative-and-non-photorealistic-volume-rendering.md)
Augments physics-based illumination pipelines with artistic techniques to enhance the perception of structure, shape, orientation, and depth [40-illustrative-and-non-photorealistic-volume-rendering.md](40-illustrative-and-non-photorealistic-volume-rendering.md). It sets itself apart by determining feature areas through continuous analysis of local volumetric properties rather than well-defined boundaries, requiring less manual tuning than traditional direct volume rendering. Choose this when physical accuracy is secondary to structural clarity.

### [Interaction](41-interaction.md)
Provides the control loop between the user and the renderer, solving the problem of static, pre-computed images by allowing real-time exploration [41-interaction.md](41-interaction.md). It differs by focusing on the manipulation of geometric, data, and visual parameters rather than the static mapping itself. Choose this for applications requiring real-time parameter adjustment and coordinated view exploration.

## Background
Not given in the sources. The concept of mapping data to visual properties originated with the development of Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) in the 1980s [G]. Early work focused on simple transfer functions to define opacity and color for scalar data [G]. The field expanded to include multi-field visualization as vector and tensor data became common in scientific computing [39-multi-field-vector-and-tensor-volume-visualization.md](39-multi-field-vector-and-tensor-volume-visualization.md). Non-photorealistic techniques were later introduced to address visual clutter in dense volumetric data [G]. Interaction frameworks evolved to support real-time parameter adjustment, becoming standard in modern visualization systems [41-interaction.md](41-interaction.md).
